name: Dutch Defense: Staunton Gambit
summary: The Staunton Gambit (1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5) sacrifices a pawn to open lines and pressure e4 against the Dutch Defense.
intro: The Staunton Gambit is White's most aggressive anti-Dutch weapon, arising after 1.d4 f5 2.e4, when the pawn offer 2...fxe4 is answered by 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5. Rather than allowing Black the customary Dutch structures, White sacrifices a central pawn to open lines, accelerate development, and exploit the slight loosening of Black's kingside caused by the early ...f5. The bishop on g5 pins the f6-knight and intensifies the pressure on the e4-pawn, which Black usually cannot comfortably keep. Named after the leading nineteenth-century English master Howard Staunton, the gambit trades material for rapid piece activity and enduring attacking chances.
line: d4 f5 e4 fxe4 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Staunton Gambit is built on speed and initiative. By giving up the e4-pawn, White opens the position before Black has developed, and the ...f5 advance means the black king's cover is slightly compromised. The pin with 4.Bg5 ties the f6-knight to the defense of the queen and adds a second attacker to e4, so Black rarely manages to hold the extra pawn for long. White's pieces flood out quickly toward f3, e2 and the centre, and the half-open lines created by the pawn sacrifice provide natural targets.

Black's task is to return the pawn at a good moment and complete development without falling into a lasting initiative against them. Careful defenders neutralize the pressure on f6 and e4, castle into relative safety, and rely on the extra structural soundness once White's attack has burned out. If Black defends precisely the material investment can tell in a long game, but a single careless move can allow White's lead in development to become decisive.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line runs 1.d4 f5 2.e4 fxe4 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5, when Black's principal reply is 4...Nc6 or the solid 4...g6, preparing to fianchetto and blunt White's initiative on the long diagonal. After 4...g6 5.f3 White strikes at the e4-pawn directly, aiming to regain it with a strong centre and open lines. Older recommendations such as 4...e6 free the f8-bishop but concede space and can leave Black passive.

A well-known aggressive attempt for Black is to cling to the extra pawn with ...d5 and ...Bf5 ideas, but this often leaves the king exposed to White's rapid development. Practice has shown that Black does best to give the pawn back and complete development harmoniously, for example with an early ...g6 and ...Bg7, reaching sound positions where White's compensation is real but not more than sufficient. Precise handling by both sides keeps the theoretical assessment close to balanced.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The gambit is named after Howard Staunton, the foremost English player of the mid-nineteenth century and widely regarded as the world's strongest master of his era. He employed the 2.e4 pawn sacrifice against the Dutch Defense, and the line has carried his name ever since. Though never a mainstream choice at the very top, the Staunton Gambit has retained a following among attacking players who wish to sidestep the heavily analyzed main Dutch systems. It remains a respected surprise weapon, prized for the practical problems it poses to an unprepared opponent.
